summary:
Title: FirePulse — Spatially & Temporally Harmonized Active-Fire Intelligence Platform

What We Developed:
We developed FirePulse, an open-source geospatial platform that harmonizes active-fire and thermal anomaly observations from NASA’s MODIS (1,000m) and VIIRS (375m) satellite sensors into a unified, cross-calibrated intelligence system.

How It Addresses the Challenge:
Raw thermal hotspot counts cannot be directly compared across sensors due to vast differences in spatial resolution, equatorial crossing times, and swath geometries. Comparing them directly creates false burning trends—VIIRS detects 3 to 4 times more thermal pixels than MODIS for the exact same fire. FirePulse solves this by ingesting NASA FIRMS feeds, projecting observations onto a standardized 1km × 1km equal-area cylindrical grid (EPSG:6933), and aggregating co-located detections into daily "active cell-days." It classifies cross-sensor co-detections and contextualizes historical trends across four distinct observational eras (MODIS baseline, early overlap, JPSS constellation, and post-Suomi-NPP).

Why It Is Important:
Wildfire risk and climate assessments require reliable, long-term trends spanning 2000 to the present without sensor-transition artifacts. FirePulse delivers mathematically rigorous, de-duplicated wildfire metrics, interactive global time-lapse playback, and API exports—equipping fire managers, climate scientists, and disaster response teams with trustworthy active-fire intelligence.
details:
Project Details: FirePulse

1. What does it do or how does it work?

FirePulse is an automated, web-based Earth Observation intelligence platform designed to eliminate spatial and temporal disparities between NASA’s legacy MODIS (1,000m) and modern VIIRS (375m) active-fire observations.

The platform operates via a four-stage pipeline:

  1. Multi-Sensor Ingestion: Ingests near-real-time (NRT) and historical thermal anomaly feeds from NASA FIRMS (Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21) via REST APIs and archive datasets.
  2. Equal-Area Geospatial Projection (EPSG:6933): Rather than relying on standard latitude/longitude grids which suffer severe area distortion towards the poles, FirePulse reprojects raw observation points onto a standardized 1km × 1km Equal-Area Cylindrical Grid.
  3. Temporal Harmonization & Co-Detection Logic: Satellite observations are binned into daily 24-hour UTC cycles ("active cell-days"). Co-located detections occurring within the same 1km cell on the same day are cross-calibrated into unified fire events, computing joint Fire Radiative Power (FRP) metrics (mean, max) and tagging whether an event was co-detected or sensor-exclusive.
  4. Interactive Analytics & Time Machine: Delivers a full analytical suite featuring interactive global maps, spatial filtering by Area of Interest (AOI), seasonal trend decomposition, sensor concordance matrices, and a lightweight 60 FPS "Time Machine" playback engine powered by dynamic 3-degree spatial binning.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates False Detection Artifacts: A single fire viewed by VIIRS often produces 3–4 adjacent 375m hotspot pixels, whereas MODIS observes it as a single 1km pixel. FirePulse standardizes both into unified 1km cell-days, preventing artificial 300%–400% wildfire increase claims.
  • Cross-Era Comparability: Bridges the historical 2000–present baseline so that pre-2012 MODIS-only records can be reliably analyzed alongside modern multi-satellite JPSS constellations.
  • High-Performance Responsiveness: Bypasses browser memory crashes by pre-aggregating 25,000+ global observations into regional geographic clusters, ensuring sub-100ms API queries and smooth animations.
  • Transparent Data Export: Provides researchers and agencies with one-click GeoJSON and CSV exports categorized by sensor dominance, co-detection confidence, and FRP.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Climate Science & Carbon Accounting: Provides climate researchers and IPCC reporting bodies with statistically consistent 25-year active-fire time series, preventing erroneous trend conclusions caused by sensor transitions.
  • Wildfire Management & First Responders: Grants regional disaster management teams a single, cross-verified operating picture that highlights high-confidence co-detections while reducing false positives.
  • Environmental Policymaking: Equips policymakers and forestry departments with verified fire seasonality data and cross-country burning comparisons to evaluate the true effectiveness of fire bans and land-use policies.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.12 (Backend & Ingestion Engine), TypeScript (Frontend).
  • Backend Architecture: Flask, SQLAlchemy ORM, SQLite with spatial indexing, NumPy, and Pandas for statistical transformations.
  • Frontend & Visualization: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet & React-Leaflet (custom canvas layers), Recharts (interactive time-series & histograms), Lucide Icons.
  • Geospatial & Remote Sensing Standards: NASA FIRMS API, NASA LANCE feeds, EPSG:6933 (NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 Global Equal-Area Cylindrical projection), WGS-84 (EPSG:4326).
  • Deployment & Cloud Infrastructure: Vercel Serverless Architecture, Git/GitHub for version control, and pre-seeded spatial databases.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Equal-Area "Cell-Day" Metrology: Instead of simply buffering points with arbitrary circular radii (which creates overlap ambiguity and polar distortion), FirePulse establishes equal-area grid cells as standard units of burning activity.
  • Dynamic Multi-Cluster Playback: Traditional web maps freeze when animating tens of thousands of global points over years. FirePulse uses a creative server-side spatial-binning algorithm that preserves continental dispersion patterns (Australia, Amazon Basin, Sahel, boreal forests) while maintaining fluid frame rates.
  • Sensor Era Awareness: FirePulse actively prevents user error by embedding satellite mission timelines directly into analytical charts (e.g., highlighting the Suomi-NPP operational decommissioning on Nov 2, 2026), ensuring historical trend analyses are scientifically defensible.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Orbital Mechanics & Diurnal Cycles: Accounted for differing equatorial crossing times—morning overpasses (Terra ~10:30 AM), afternoon overpasses (Aqua & Suomi-NPP ~1:30 PM), and offset orbits (NOAA-20 at 12:45 PM)—which capture distinct phases of daily wildfire intensity.
  • Scan Geometry & Off-Nadir Distortion: Acknowledged MODIS "bow-tie" pixel growth (from 1km at nadir up to ~4.8km at swath edges) versus VIIRS onboard pixel trimming and aggregation.
  • Operational Reality & Serverless Boundaries: Designed the data storage and ingestion pipelines to operate reliably within serverless execution constraints, handling ephemeral environments, read-only file systems, and API rate limits without service disruption.
